prompt: Why does a production prompt live in one file with a history, rather than one file per version?
hint: Think about the program that reads it.

choices.text: Git refuses to store more than one prompt file in a directory
choices.why: Git stores as many files as you like; the lab has twenty prompts in one directory.

choices.text: The program reads one path, and git records which text was live and when
choices.why: Right. A directory of versions leaves somebody to choose, and records nothing about the choice.

choices.text: Separate files make every call cost more tokens, because each one is sent along
choices.why: Only the prompt that is sent costs tokens, wherever it is stored.

choices.text: A single file is loaded faster by the program, so each call returns sooner
choices.why: Where a prompt is stored has nothing to do with how fast a call is.

prompt: Why are the commit hashes in this lesson the same as the ones you get when you rebuild the lab?
hint: What does `lab.sh` write beside each version?

choices.text: Git numbers commits in order
choices.why: A hash is computed from the content, the author and the dates, not counted.

choices.text: The course ships a copy of its own `.git` directory inside `lab.sh`
choices.why: `lab.sh` writes each file and commits it; there is no copied repository.

choices.text: The dates and the author are set by the script, so every input to the hash is fixed
choices.why: Right. Same content, same author, same dates, same hash.

choices.text: Hashes ignore dates
choices.why: They include them, which is why the dates had to be set.

prompt: What does `git diff 9683448 931c548 -- prompts/triage.txt` tell you that the two commit messages do not?
hint: A message says what somebody meant to do.

choices.text: Whether the change improved the score
choices.why: Nothing in git knows the score; that needs a run.

choices.text: Who approved the change
choices.why: A diff shows lines, not approvals.

choices.text: Exactly which lines were added and removed
choices.why: Right: the message is the intention, the diff is the change.

choices.text: How many tokens the new version costs on every call to the model
choices.why: That is `pl tokens` or `pl log`, not a diff.

prompt: To print the file as it was at commit `c8470c9`, you run `git ___ c8470c9:prompts/triage.txt`.
hint: The same subcommand prints a commit with its diff.

prompt: `pl run` printed the id `c1916fcd` for today's file and for the copy taken from commit `c8470c9`. Why are they equal?
hint: The id is a hash of something.

choices.text: The harness caches ids by file name
choices.why: The two files had different names and still got one id.

choices.text: Every byte is the same
choices.why: Right. The diff between the commits has no lines, and the id is a hash of the bytes.

choices.text: The id is the date of the newest commit
choices.why: It is the start of a SHA-256 of the file.

choices.text: Both runs used the same test set
choices.why: The test set is not part of the prompt id.

prompt: Running `prompts/triage.txt` with `--set temperature=0.8` kept the id `c1916fcd`. How many of the 40 dev messages passed everything?
hint: The `all` row of `pl check runs/hot.jsonl`.

prompt: Why should `temperature` be written above the `---` in the prompt file rather than passed with `--set`?
hint: What does the id see?

choices.text: `--set` is ignored by the stand-in
choices.why: It is not ignored: the score fell from 36 to 28.

choices.text: In the file it is part of the hashed bytes, so a change to it changes the id
choices.why: Right. On the command line it belongs to one run and nothing records it.

choices.text: The header makes calls cheaper
choices.why: Where a setting is written does not change what a call costs.

choices.text: `--set` only accepts whole numbers
choices.why: It accepted 0.8.

prompt: Which of these belong to a version of a prompt, in the lesson's sense? Choose all that apply.
hint: Four things.

choices.text: The text of the file
choices.why: Yes, and git tracks it.

choices.text: The model it is sent to
choices.why: Yes: the same text on another model is another prompt.

choices.text: The test set its score was measured on
choices.why: Yes: a score belongs to a pair.

choices.text: The name of the person who committed it
choices.why: Git records it, but it does not change what the prompt does.

prompt: A provider moves a short model alias to a newer model. Your prompt file names the alias and has not changed. What has happened to your version?
hint: The text is half of what produces the answer.

choices.text: Nothing, because the prompt id did not change
choices.why: The id covers the file; the model behind the alias is outside it.

choices.text: It is a new version that no commit records
choices.why: Right. Naming the dated model in the header turns that move into a visible commit.

choices.text: The provider has to send you a diff
choices.why: No provider can diff your prompt; nothing in your repository changed.

choices.text: Only the cost changed
choices.why: The answers can change too: the model is half of what produces them.

prompt: What does `pl log` print for each commit of `prompts/triage.txt`?
hint: Two numbers, and where they come from.

choices.text: The number of lines the commit changed
choices.why: That is `git show --stat`, not `pl log`.

choices.text: A score and its tokens
choices.why: Right: it runs each version, it does not read old results.

choices.text: The prompt id only
choices.why: It prints the passes and the tokens beside the subject.

choices.text: Who reviewed each change
choices.why: Nothing in the lab records a review.

prompt: `9683448` used 11636 tokens over the forty dev calls and `f361c0a` used 11036. How many extra tokens per call did the new instruction add?
hint: Subtract, then divide by the number of calls.

prompt: `931c548` added 1720 tokens on dev and left the score at 36 of 40. What did `pl log cases/attacks.jsonl` show about it?
hint: Dev does not test what the change was for.

choices.text: Nothing changed there either
choices.why: It went from 1 to 6 of 10.

choices.text: It broke every attack
choices.why: That was `31a6a59`, at 0 of 10.

choices.text: It took the attacks from 1 of 10 to 6
choices.why: Right: its tokens bought something dev cannot see.

choices.text: It made the attack set cheaper to run than before
choices.why: Tokens rose from 2818 to 3302.

prompt: Why did `31a6a59` take the score to zero although the instruction to reply with JSON was still in the prompt?
hint: Lesson 1: which wins, a description or an example?

choices.text: The stand-in copies the shape of the first example, and the examples were no longer JSON
choices.why: Right. The example disagreed with the description and won.

choices.text: The prompt became too long for the model
choices.why: It became shorter: 9739 tokens against 13356.

choices.text: The message tags were removed
choices.why: The diff touches only the three `Output:` lines.

choices.text: Temperature was raised
choices.why: No parameter changed in that commit.

prompt: A change leaves every test set's score where it was and adds 40 tokens per call. What does the lesson say to do?
hint: A change no test set can see is taken on trust.

choices.text: Merge it, since nothing broke
choices.why: Nothing broke and nothing was shown to improve; the tokens are paid on every call.

choices.text: Revert it at once, because a change that moves no score is always wrong
choices.why: It may fix something real that no case tests yet.

choices.text: Run it again, a few more times, until one of the scores moves and settles the question
choices.why: At temperature 0 the stand-in answers the same way every time.

choices.text: Add a case that shows what it fixes, or record that it fixes nothing measurable
choices.why: Right. Either way the next reader knows what the tokens are for.

prompt: In the gate the lesson describes, which line of `pl compare` decides whether a change is stopped?
hint: A total can stay put while one message is fixed and another broken.

choices.text: The total of passes
choices.why: A total hides a swap of one fixed for one broken.

choices.text: The `broken` line
choices.why: Right: it names every message the change broke.

choices.text: The p value of the sign test
choices.why: One broken message matters even when the p value says nothing.

choices.text: The prompt id of the newer run
choices.why: The id says which file ran, not whether it got worse.

prompt: Comparing `c8470c9` with `31a6a59` on dev, how many messages did `pl compare` list as broken?
hint: The `broken` count.

prompt: The run at temperature 0.8 broke eight messages. Why would a gate that runs only when the prompt file changes miss it?
hint: Where was the change?

choices.text: Because eight is too few to count
choices.why: The sign test put it at 0.008.

choices.text: Because sampling makes every run different
choices.why: That explains the answers, not why the gate would not run.

choices.text: The file never changed
choices.why: Right. With every parameter in the file, every change is a change to the file.

choices.text: Because `pl compare` ignores the temperature
choices.why: It compared the two runs and found the eight.

prompt: Which of these belong to the gate the section describes? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three parts, none of them clever.

choices.text: It runs on every change to a prompt file, before the merge
choices.why: Yes: a check somebody has to remember runs on the days they remember.

choices.text: It runs every test set the prompt has
choices.why: Yes: dev alone is blind to what the attack set sees.

choices.text: It fails on any broken message and prints the ids
choices.why: Yes, and a merge anyway is explained in the commit.

choices.text: It runs once a week on the live prompt
choices.why: A weekly run finds the regression days late, as August did.

prompt: Put these steps for a change to `prompts/triage.txt` in the order the lesson implies.
hint: The gate runs before anything reaches production.
items: Run the new file and the live one over every test set
Compare the runs and read the broken messages
Merge, or explain in the commit why a broken message is acceptable

prompt: Match each commit to what `pl log` showed about it.
hint: Read the two columns down.

pairs.right: Score up from 24 to 36, tokens more than doubled
Tokens up, no score moved on any set shown
Flat on dev, 1 to 6 on the attacks

prompt: A teammate reports 36 of 40 for 'the triage prompt' in a chat message, with no id. What is missing before anybody can rebuild that result?
hint: Four things make a version.

choices.text: Only the date of the message, since the history then shows which commit was live that day
choices.why: A date does not say which text, settings, model or test set produced it.

choices.text: The file's id with its parameters, the model, and which test set at which commit
choices.why: Right: without all four, the number is about something nobody can rebuild.

choices.text: The sign test's p value
choices.why: A p value compares two runs; it does not identify one.

choices.text: A screenshot of the output, so that nobody can retype any of the numbers wrongly later
choices.why: A picture of the number is the same number with the same gaps.
